text: Nine chapters of comparison can't cover every function, every edge case, on every platform, forever -- and this course doesn't try to. What it can leave you with is the right habit: knowing exactly which source to open first for each dialect you'll actually work in, and how to read that source correctly once you're there.

Five references worth bookmarking right now, one per platform category this course covered. Learn dot microsoft dot com for T-SQL -- Microsoft's official reference, versioned by SQL Server release and by Azure SQL. Docs dot oracle dot com for PL/SQL -- Oracle's official Database SQL and PL/SQL Language References, versioned by database release. Dev dot mysql dot com slash doc slash refman for MySQL -- the official Reference Manual, versioned per major release. Postgresql dot org slash docs for PostgreSQL. And for the cloud warehouses this course briefly introduced -- Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery, Redshift -- each vendor's own official docs site.

PostgreSQL's documentation deserves a specific callout of its own. It is widely regarded as some of the best technical documentation anywhere in the open-source world -- not just adequate, genuinely thorough, with real worked examples for nearly every function, and a clear, consistent structure across releases. If you remember exactly one specific recommendation from this lesson, remember this: postgresql dot org slash docs is worth opening even when you're not sure PostgreSQL has the answer. It usually does, and it usually explains it well.

But the habit that matters more than any single bookmark is this: before trusting any doc page, ask whether it actually matches the version and edition you're running against. This isn't hypothetical -- you've already seen it directly, more than once, in this course. MySQL 8.0 added CTEs and window functions that simply didn't exist before, which the capstone lesson depended on directly. MySQL's sql_mode defaults tightened starting at version 5.7. Oracle has introduced genuinely new PL/SQL capabilities release by release. A doc page you open without checking its version can describe behavior your actual database doesn't have, or leave out a feature it does have.

So: five authoritative sources, one per platform category, and one habit that matters more than any of them -- always match the version of the docs to the version you're actually running. Next lesson is the last one in this entire course: a genuine wrap-up of the single throughline connecting everything you've learned across all ten chapters. See you there.
